```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false


 # 1. ENP per Post  
  ward.level |> 
    group_by(year, code_fe, post) |> 
    mutate(p_share = vote/sum(vote), na.rm = T) |> 
    summarise(
      ENP_post = 1/sum(p_share^2), 
      totalVote = sum(vote),
      .groups = "drop") -> enp_post

  # 2. ENP per ward (normalised)
  enp_post |> 
    group_by(year, code_fe) |> 
    summarise(ENP_raw = mean(ENP_post, na.rm = T), .groups = "drop") |> 
    mutate(ENP_norm = rescale(ENP_raw, to = c(0,1))) -> enp_ward

  # 3. Compute MoV raw
  ward.level %>%
    select(year, province_no, party, code_fe, vote, post, lg_consti, WardNo) |> 
    group_by(year, post, code_fe) |> 
    arrange(desc(vote), .by_group = TRUE) |> 
    mutate(percent = vote / sum(vote) * 100) |> 
    summarise(
      MoV = percent[1] - ifelse(n() >= 2, percent[2], 0), # if only 1 candidate, second = 0
      totalVote = sum(vote),
      dominant_party_post = party[1],
      .groups = "drop"
    ) -> ward.mov
    
  # 4. Ward-level totals by party (needed to pick dominant_party_ward by total votes)
  ward_party_totals <- ward.level |> 
    filter(!is.na(WardNo)) |> 
    group_by(year, code_fe, party) |> 
    summarise(totalVote_party = sum(vote), .groups = "drop")


# 5. Compute MoV (weighted) and ILV (SD of MoV per post)
  ward.mov |> 
    group_by(year, code_fe) |> 
    summarise(
      ward_MoV_raw = weighted.mean(MoV, totalVote, na.rm = TRUE),
      ILV_raw = sd(MoV, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop") |> 
    mutate(
      MoV_norm = rescale(ward_MoV_raw, to = c(0, 1)),
      ILV_norm = rescale(ILV_raw, to = c(0, 1))
    ) -> mov_ilv
  
# 6. Merge ENP + MoV + ILV
ward_df <- enp_ward |> 
  left_join(mov_ilv, by = c("year", "code_fe")) %>%
  mutate(
    WOI_base = (ENP_norm + (1 - MoV_norm) + ILV_norm) / 3,
    WOI_weight =  0.5 * (1 - MoV_norm) +
      0.3 * ENP_norm +
      0.2 * ILV_norm
  )

  ward_df |> 
    filter(year == "79") |> 
    mutate(
      abs_cat = case_when(
        WOI_weight >= 0.65 ~ "A",
        WOI_weight >= 0.50 ~ "B",
        WOI_weight >= 0.35 ~ "C",
        TRUE ~ "D"
      ),
      p_rank = percent_rank(WOI_weight),
      percent_cat = case_when(
        p_rank >= 0.75 ~ "A", 
        p_rank >= 0.50  ~ "B",
        p_rank >= 0.25 ~ "C",
        TRUE ~ "D"
      )
    ) -> indicators



indicators |> 
  left_join(
    fe_name |> 
      select(code_fe, name), by = "code_fe"
  ) -> indicators
```

# Diagnostic Analysis of Past Election Results

In this section we will analyse the electoral landscape of the Lalitpur - 3 based on past two election at federal, provincial and local level. It attempts diagnoses past election outcomes to understand how votes were distributed, transferred, and consolidated across parties and candidates. It establishes the empirical foundation upon which the strategic analysis in later sections is built.

```{r}
  tab_options(table.align='left')
```

<br>

<br>

**Observation** : Making sense of electoral win of Ms Toshima Karki

-   Bibeksheel Sajha managed to get 12.9% vote in the election of 2074. This in intself is an indication of demand for newer face in the constituency !

-   NC, which was a significant political force, opted to support CPN-Moaist candidate in the election.

Beside other obvious and immediate political circumstances, above two reasons provided an impetus to RSP resulting a big margin of victory, which otherwise, could have been a tight race.
:::
:::::

<br>

## Voter Base of Major Political Parties

### Compare PR and FPTP votes of 2079 election

::::: grid
::: g-col-6
**Observation**

-   The diffence in votes (PR Vs FPTP) for RSP is highest. Ms Karki recieved \~27% more votes in FPTP than RSP recieved in the PR. *This substantiates the initial claim made earlier about possible swing votes from NC supports shifting to RSP in FPTP election.*

-   UML's vote share of 22.72% in FPTP and 20.44% in PR seems linear, hence can be argued that UML didnt undperform in the fptp election.

-   Similarly, Maoist got 5% more vote in FPTP than in PR - we can presume that at least 50% of such votes that it got in FPTP (\~4000) should be from NC supporters. While the alliance failed miserably in terms of transfering vote from NC to Maoist, the performance of Maoist should be considered *okayis* and not bad in the elction of fptp.

-   It is evident that the significant portion of \~14% vote that NC recieved in FPTP got transferred to RSP in FPTP along with 10% votes of RPP and additional 7% recieved by parties in PR election who had no representation in FPTP.

-   **At least 35% voters with leftist inclination**

-   Candidate selections from NC and RPP will largely determine what happens with RSP or any similar forces in this constituency.

### Estimating voter base of major Political party from local elections - 2079

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12

ward.level |>

                        )

    y = "",

  )+

  ) +

    ),
    plot.margin = margin(

    ),
    axis.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

```

The local election is a loose but a evidence driven indicator of voter landscape for legacy political parties. It can also be used to serve to analyse indicative ideological inclination of voters at large.

@fig-wardelection suggests a clear left inclined constituency with right wing and centerist or center to left party as strong contendors. Furthermore,

-   The average vote recieved by the parties at ward level is also in line with the vote received by parties in the FPTP electin of 2074 as shown in @tbl-results-fptp.

-   This further supports the claim that the left vote has more or less tranfered to FPTP (though distributed among left parties) and also that the CPN UML's electoral performance of FPTP in 2079 should be considered satisfactory.

# Electoral Opportunity & Strategic Landscape - Direction for the way ahead !

This section provides a **strategic reading of the constituency’s electoral landscape**, focusing on where political competition exists and where it does not. Instead of treating the constituency as a single homogeneous unit, the analysis breaks it down ward-by-ward to assess fragmentation, competitiveness, and voter volatility.

The indicators presented here—ENP, MoV, ILV, and the Composite Index—are designed to answer three practical campaign questions:

-   Where are voters most open to alternatives?
-   Where are margins narrow enough to realistically flip?
-   Where does volatility suggest weak party consolidation?

The output is a clear prioritisation of wards, enabling evidence-based campaign planning rather than intuition-driven targeting.

## ENP - Effective Number of Parties

**Concept**

ENP measures party fragmentation — how many parties are effectively competing in a constituency, weighted by their vote share.

Low ENP → few dominant parties

High ENP → many parties with similar vote shares

**Strategic Value**

1.  Comparative Evaluation of general party fragmentation among other constituency or at ward level.

2.  Prepare ward-level strategy

    -   Wards with high ENP suggests marginal or small disruption creates a greater impact for new entrants -- Non polarised voter signals opportunity for new ideas and ppl.

    -   Ward with low ENP : Strategise based on people's percieved grievances against establashed dominant parties.

3.  Identify wards or segments of wards (such as provincial constituency) with high ENP that gives a good entry point for new entrants

4.  Uniform political campaign strategy for groups of wards (as categories in @tbl-category-enp)

```{r}
  summarise(

  opt_table_lines()
```

:::
:::::

Maps above (@fig-map-enp-ward) has ENP values derived from local elections for each ward; it ranges from 2.5 to 5.8. Higher ENP suggests higher voter fragmentation (means major party has no stronghold and/or consolidated) and lower ENP suggests voter consoldiation and lower voter fragmentation (anything lower than 2.5 is effectively a bipolar race).

Based on the ENP values @fig-map-enp-ward-cat illustrates a priority category for the new party. Below @tbl-category-enp provides list of wards based on cateogory of prioritisation. \[*please note that **Priority 1** in this report suggests wards that should be considered the favourable condition for the new entrants*\]

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| label: tbl-category-enp
#| tbl-cap: List of wards based on ENP category 


indicators |> 
  mutate(
    category = case_when(
      ENP_raw > 5 ~ "Priority A",
      ENP_raw > 4 & ENP_raw < 5 ~ "Priority B",
      ENP_raw > 3 & ENP_raw < 4 ~ "Priority C",
      .default = "Priority D"
      )
    ) |>
  filter(year == "79") |> 
  select(code_fe, category, name) |> 
  group_by(category) |> 
  arrange(code_fe) |> 
  summarise(name = str_c(name, collapse = ","), .groups = "drop") |>
  gt() |>
  opt_table_lines() 
  




```

## Indicator II : Margin of Victory (MoV)

**Concept**

MoV reflects **competitiveness**. It is calcuated as a differece (in percentage point of vote share) between the winner and runner-up (rank 1 and 2).

Smaller MoV -\> Higher chances of contestability or voters are tightly divided

Larger MoV -\> Strong dominance by a single party or voters significantly more inclined towards a dominant party.

**Strategic Value**

1.  The federal MoV, at prime facie, a measure how tightly the constituency is contested with. Lower MoV value is a favourable condition, at large, for the new entrants

2.  Identify segments of wards or invidiual wards with similar traits to formulate similar plans :

    a.  For example in wards with Lower MoV: Higher chances of contestability
    b.  In case of ward with higher MoV: suggests strong dominance by a single party and hence the startegy could be combination of anti-incumbency agendas along with other relevant measures based on the dominant party.

<br>

### MoV - Local Level

```{r}
#| echo: false

# 1) MoV per post × ward (same idea as your original)

per_post <- ward.level %>%
  #filter(!is.na(WardNo)) %>%
  #mutate(code_fe = paste(lg_code, WardNo, sep = "-")) %>%
  select(year, province_no, party, code_fe, vote, post, lg_consti, WardNo) %>%
  #group_by(year, post, code_fe, party) %>%
  #summarise(vote = sum(vote), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(year, post, code_fe) %>%
  arrange(desc(vote), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(percent = vote / sum(vote) * 100) %>%
  summarise(
    MoV = percent[1] - ifelse(n() >= 2, percent[2], 0), # if only 1 candidate, second = 0
    totalVote = sum(vote),
    dominant_party_post = party[1],
    .groups = "drop"
  )


# 2) Ward-level totals by party (needed to pick dominant_party_ward by total votes)
ward_party_totals <- ward.level %>%
  filter(!is.na(WardNo)) %>%
  mutate(code_fe = paste(lg_code, WardNo, sep = "-")) %>%
  group_by(year, code_fe, party) %>%
  summarise(totalVote_party = sum(vote), .groups = "drop")

# 3) Ward-level summary: ward_MoV (weighted by post total votes) + dominant_party_ward (by total votes)
ward_summary <- per_post %>%
  group_by(year, code_fe) %>%
  reframe(
    ILV = sd(MoV, na.rm = TRUE),
    ward_MoV = weighted.mean(MoV, totalVote, na.rm = TRUE),
    totalVote_ward = sum(totalVote)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  left_join(
    ward_party_totals %>%
      group_by(year, code_fe) %>%
      slice_max(totalVote_party, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
      rename(dominant_party_ward = party) %>%
      select(year, code_fe, dominant_party_ward, totalVote_party),
    by = c("year", "code_fe")
  ) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(
    # Normalize ILV and MoV within each year
    ILV_norm = (ILV - min(ILV, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(ILV, na.rm = TRUE) - min(ILV, na.rm = TRUE)),
    MoV_norm = (ward_MoV - min(ward_MoV, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(ward_MoV, na.rm = TRUE) - min(ward_MoV, na.rm = TRUE)),
    
    # Composite Window Index
    CWI = 0.6*(1 - MoV_norm) + (0.4 * ILV_norm),
    CWI = round(CWI, 3)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# 4) Constituency-level aggregation: weighted MoV and dominant party by summed votes across wards
constituency_summary <- ward_summary %>%
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarise(
    constituency_MoV = weighted.mean(ward_MoV, totalVote_ward, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  # compute dominant party across wards by summing ward total votes by party
  bind_cols(
    ward_summary %>%
      group_by(dominant_party_ward) %>%
      summarise(votes_by_party = sum(totalVote_ward), .groups = "drop") %>%
      slice_max(votes_by_party, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
      transmute(dominant_party_constituency = dominant_party_ward)
  )

ward_summary |> 
  group_by(year) %>%  # normalize within each election year
  mutate(
    NMoV = (ward_MoV - min(ward_MoV, na.rm = TRUE)) / 
           (max(ward_MoV, na.rm = TRUE) - min(ward_MoV, na.rm = TRUE))
  ) |> 
  ungroup() -> nMoV_ward
```

### MoV under microscope - Intra-Local Volatality (ILV)

**Concept**

ILV measures **how much voter preference fluctuates** within a ward across elections.

Higher ILV → Suggests higher fluctuation Lower ILV → Suggest lower flucturation

**Strategic Value**

1.  ILV is a measure of spread of MoV values within each ward. Generally, higher ILV (higher flactuation) provides strategic advantage for new political options as voters have not consolidated to any political force.

2.  ILV along with MoV (for each ward) can be used to identify individual wards with strategic values and formulate campaigns plans accordingly.

### Winnability Index (Composite Index of ILV and MoV)

<br>

The winnability Index is a composite index of ILV and MoV that are combined to provide a single actionable indicator.

The first set of figures below (@fig-hybrid-list and @fig-map-cwi) categories wards based on absolute value of composite index. In this case, there are 4 wards that are categoriesed as top up-for-grabs for new political party.

<br>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fn-hyprid-ILV-MoV

indicators |> 
  #filter(year == "79") |> 
  select(year, code_fe, MoV_norm, ILV_norm, name) |> 
  mutate(
    # --- Step 1: Compute CWI ---
    CWI = 0.6*(1 - MoV_norm) + 0.4 * ILV_norm,
    CWI = round(CWI, 3),

    # --- Step 2: Absolute thresholds ---
    abs_cat = case_when(
      CWI >= 0.75 ~ "A",
      CWI >= 0.50 ~ "B",
      CWI >= 0.25 ~ "C",
      CWI < 0.25 ~ "D"
    ),
    # --- Step 3: Percentile rank category ---
    pct_rank = percent_rank(CWI),
    pct_cat = case_when(
      pct_rank >= 0.75 ~ "A",
      pct_rank >= 0.50 ~ "B",
      pct_rank >= 0.25 ~ "C",
      pct_rank < 0.25 ~ "D"
    )
  ) |> 
  # --- Step 4: Hybrid adjustment ---
  group_by(year) |> 
  mutate(
    # Count A wards in absolute categorisation
    num_A = sum(abs_cat == "A"),
    pct_A = sum(pct_cat == "A"),
    compare = 0.10*pct_A > num_A,
    # If no A from abs_cat, promote top 10% (pct_rank >= 0.90)
    hybrid_cat = case_when(
      compare == T & pct_rank >= 0.90 ~ "A",
     # num_A == 0                   ~ pct_cat,    # fallback to percentile category
      TRUE                         ~ abs_cat     # default absolute category
    )
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  select(-num_A, -pct_A, -compare) -> hybrid




```

## Ward-Level KPI Table: ILV, MoV & Composite Indicator

This table provides a ward-by-ward summary of electoral dynamics.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

voter |> 
  count(code_fe, name = "total") |> 
  mutate(vote_share = total/sum(total)*100) |> 
  select(-total) -> vote.to.join

ward.level |> 
  filter(year == "79") |> 
  # filter(post  "दलित महिला सदस्य") |> 
  group_by(code_fe, post) |> 
  mutate(vote_share_nc = vote/sum(vote)*100) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  filter(party == "नेपाली काँग्रेस") |> 
  select(code_fe, vote, vote_share_nc, post) -> nc_vote_share


nc_vote_share |> 
  group_by(code_fe) |>
  mutate(
    vote_share = coalesce(
      vote_share_nc[post == "दलित महिला सदस्य"][1],
      vote_share_nc[post == "महिला सदस्य"][1],
      vote_share_nc[post == "वडा अध्यक्ष"][1]
    )
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    vote_number = coalesce(
      vote[post == "दलित महिला सदस्य"][1],
      vote[post == "महिला सदस्य"][1],
      vote[post == "वडा सदस्य"][1])
  ) -> nc_vote_share

 


  vote.to.join |> 
    left_join(
      nc_vote_share |> 
        select(code_fe, vote_share, vote_number) |> rename("nc_vote_share" = "vote_share")
        |> unique(), by = "code_fe"
    ) |> 
    left_join(
      ward_party_totals |> 
        filter(year == "79") |> 
        group_by(code_fe) |> 
        filter(totalVote_party == max(totalVote_party)) |> 
        select(code_fe, party) |> rename("dominant_party" = "party"), by = "code_fe"
    ) -> vote.to.join


# 1. Logic Flip & Highlighting
table_data <- indicators |> 
  filter(year == "79") |> 
  left_join(vote.to.join, by = "code_fe") |> 
  mutate(
    # Flipping Priority: A becomes D (Stronghold), D becomes A (Target)
    nc_priority = case_when(
      percent_cat == "A" ~ "D: Expansion Target",
      percent_cat == "B" ~ "C: Lean Opportunity",
      percent_cat == "C" ~ "B: Lean Stronghold",
      percent_cat == "D" ~ "A: Core Stronghold",
      .default = percent_cat
    ),
    # Identify "Anomalies": NC is dominant but Index is low (Fragile Strongholds)
    status_alert = ifelse(dominant_party == "नेपाली काँग्रेस" & WOI_weight < median(WOI_weight, na.rm=T), 
                          "⚠️ High Risk", "Stable")
  ) |> 
  arrange(nc_priority) # Sort by new NC priority

# 2. The Final Aesthetic GT Table
table_data |> 
  select(name, dominant_party, ENP_raw, ward_MoV_raw, ILV_raw, 
         WOI_weight, nc_priority, vote_share, nc_vote_share, vote_number) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title  = md("**NC Strategic Ward Management**"),
    subtitle = "Reversed Priority: Core Strongholds (A) vs. Expansion Targets (D)"
  ) |> 
  
  # A. Number Formatting
  fmt_number(columns = c(ENP_raw, ward_MoV_raw, ILV_raw, WOI_weight), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = vote_number, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(vote_share, nc_vote_share), scale_values = FALSE, decimals = 2) |>

  # B. Conditional Color Palette for NC Strongholds
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#1A5276"), cell_text(color = "white", weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = nc_priority == "A: Core Stronghold")
  ) |> 
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#AED6F1")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = nc_priority == "B: Lean Stronghold")
  ) |> 
  
  # C. Highlight the "Fragile" NC Wards (The "Anomaly" you asked for)
  # tab_style(
  #   style = list(cell_text(color = "red", weight = "bold")),
  #   locations = cells_body(columns = status_alert, rows = status_alert == "⚠️ High Risk")
  # ) |> 
  
  # D. High-Contrast Opportunity Heatmap
  data_color(
    columns = WOI_weight,
    palette = "viridis", # Different palette to distinguish from previous version
    alpha = 0.8,
    autocolor_text = TRUE
  ) |> 

  cols_label(
    name = "Ward", 
    dominant_party = "Current Dominant",
    nc_priority = "NC Priority Class",
    WOI_weight = "Risk Index",
    vote_number = "NC Total Votes",
    ENP_raw = "ENP",
    ward_MoV_raw = "MoV",
    ILV_raw = "ILV",
    vote_share = "Total Voters",
    nc_vote_share = "NC vote %"
  ) |> 
  opt_table_lines() |>
  tab_options(
    column_labels.background.color = "#154360",
    table.font.size = px(12)
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false


final_nc_dashboard <- indicators |> 
  filter(year == "79") |> 
  left_join(vote.to.join, by = "code_fe") |> 
  mutate(
    # 1. Critical Calculations
    opp_total_share = vote_share - nc_vote_share,
    is_nc = ifelse(dominant_party == "नेपाली काँग्रेस", TRUE, FALSE),
    
    # 2. Safety Margin (Lead minus Volatility)
    # A negative safety margin means the 'swing' is bigger than your lead.
    safety_margin = ward_MoV_raw - ILV_raw,
    
    # 3. The Voter Gap (Target for ground teams)
    voter_gap = ifelse(is_nc & safety_margin < 0, 
                       round((abs(safety_margin)/100) * (vote_number / (nc_vote_share/100))), 
                       0),
    
    # 4. Critical Logic Labels
    nc_status = case_when(
      !is_nc & WOI_weight > 60 ~ "OFFENSE: Capture Target",
      is_nc & safety_margin < 0 ~ "CRITICAL: Under-threat",
      is_nc & opp_total_share > nc_vote_share ~ "WARNING: Split Vote Risk",
      is_nc ~ "STABLE: Stronghold",
      TRUE ~ "Observe"
    )
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(voter_gap), safety_margin)

final_nc_dashboard |> 
  select(name, dominant_party, nc_status, safety_margin, voter_gap, 
         nc_vote_share, ENP_raw, vote_number) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = md("**2026 Election: NC Strategic Defense Dashboard**"),
    subtitle = "Prioritizing Voter Retention and Fragile Strongholds"
  ) |> 
  
  # 1. Formatting
  fmt_number(columns = c(safety_margin, ENP_raw), decimals = 2) |> 
  fmt_number(columns = c(voter_gap, vote_number), decimals = 0) |> 
  fmt_percent(columns = nc_vote_share, scale_values = FALSE, decimals = 1) |> 
  
  # 2. Aesthetics: Row Highlighting for Status
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#F9EBEA"), cell_text(color = "#943126", weight = "bold")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = nc_status == "CRITICAL: Under-threat")
  ) |> 
  tab_style(
    style = list(cell_fill(color = "#FEF9E7")),
    locations = cells_body(rows = nc_status == "WARNING: Split Vote Risk")
  ) |> 
  
  # 3. The "Voter Gap" Heatmap (The Target)
  data_color(
    columns = voter_gap,
    palette = "Reds",
    domain = c(1, max(final_nc_dashboard$voter_gap))
  ) |> 
  
  # 4. Safety Margin Indicators
  data_color(
    columns = safety_margin,
    palette = "RdYlGn",
    domain = c(-15, 15)
  ) |> 

  # Labels & Styling
  cols_label(
    name = "Ward",
    dominant_party = "Current Lead",
    nc_status = "Action Status",
    safety_margin = "Safety Margin %",
    voter_gap = "Votes to Secure",
    nc_vote_share = "NC Share",
    vote_number = "Base Votes"
  ) |> 
  tab_options(
    column_labels.background.color = "#1B4F72", # NC Dark Blue
    column_labels.font.size = px(13),
    heading.title.font.size = px(22),
    table.width = pct(100)
  ) |> 
  tab_source_note(md("**Safety Margin:** Lead % minus Volatility %. **Votes to Secure:** Ground-team target to reach statistical safety.")) |> 
  opt_table_outline()
```
